body.text: In short:
A pilot program in Beijing is issuing identification cards for AI digital humans.
The ID states a name, birthday, address and facial features, and allows the digital human to own a digital currency wallet.
What's next?
Digital humans are widely used in Chinese media with the market estimated to be worth $10 billion in 2025.
Yuri was just one year old when thousands of fans gathered in Shanghai to watch her sing live.
Appearing as a female adult on a 100-metre-wide screen in a concert hall on the Bund, she sang in Mandarin and English, and changed her outfits in an instant.
Except Yuri is not a real human — she is an AI-generated virtual idol.
Earlier this year she became the first Chinese digital human to receive a government-based official identification card that states her name, birthday, address and facial features.
The official identity allows her operators to open a digital currency wallet for her business and secure commercial partnerships in industries including fashion, gaming and automotive.
The pilot program in Beijing also made her the first licensed AI artist in the country.
According to a 2025 report from the Communication University of China there are least 1.3 million firms in China linked to the digital human sector.
Last month, Beijing issued a new practice guide for broadcasting and online video services, urging them to register their digital humans.

It comes as multiple government agencies rolled out plans to regulate the avatars following President Xi Jinping's initiative to develop "new quality productive forces" and strengthen the country's self-reliance on AI.
Supporters argue it would protect intellectual property and curb online scams, while critics say it strengthens state surveillance in the metaverse.
Growing uses for AI humans
Digital humans have been widely used in China's broadcasting, online streaming, micro dramas, e-commerce and propaganda.
The market was estimated at 48 billion yuan ($10 billion) in 2025 and rapidly expanding.
It started from people using digital avatars to conceal their identities in vertical videos or live streaming as a way to keep their opinion anonymous.
With the development of machine learning, digital humans have evolved from script-reading anchors into AI-generated influencers who can interact with users in real time.
Yuri, who has 100,000 fans on Little Red Book, or RedNote, has become one of China's most popular AI influencers and is considered a pioneer in generative AI-created virtual idols.
A human team develops and maintains her system and manages her interactions with fans.
In comparison, the voice or face of many other digital influencers are adopted from real humans, according to the Chinese Digital Human Influence Index Report.
AI digital humans have gained significant traction in China's lucrative live-streaming industry, because it offers 24/7 companionship at low cost.
Beijing has also deployed its own virtual humans to convey political directives and deliver ideological and history education to Chinese Communist Party (CCP) members.
Dozens of local government agencies are also rolling out their digital human officers to respond to public inquiries.
Last year Beijing deployed two digital humans to discuss the annual Government Work Report — its annual policy statement.
It marked the first time AI avatars had been used for the country's biggest political meetings.
Speeding up legal frameworks
While the use of AI humans is growing, the industry has also drawn increasing scrutiny.
State-owned media has reported that AI digital humans posing as doctors had been used in videos to promote false medical advice.
Earlier this year an advertisement featuring an AI digital human influencer was taken down after netizens questioned how she could claim a pair of contact lenses were "comfortable".
Chinese celebrities have also had their faces and voices used without permission to create pornographic deepfakes and unauthorised online commercials.
Some companies have reportedly offered unusual deals, paying everyday people up to $20,000 to license their identities for digital human productions.
Other than Beijing's new ID system, Shanghai authorities in 2024 pioneered a blockchain framework for identifying digital humans with a permanent "serial number".
However, China has not introduced a unified national system to police the booming industry.

Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said companies should be made accountable because digital humans could not be sued or sent to prison.
"It has no moral sense, at least at the moment, of right and wrong," Dr Paterson said.
"Digital identification is a way of tracing that wrongdoing to the company that's made it available."
However, Lennon Chang, a cyber security expert from Deakin University, said the ID registration could also unmask anonymity.
This means businesses could face greater pressure to self-censor, further constraining freedom of speech in an already tightly controlled online environment, he added.
"They would definitely come with a chilling effect,"
he said.
"People won't be able to talk about those sensitive issues, even in the private space.
"Under the national security laws [the government] can do whatever they want."
